Original Passage
Language is the main means of communication between peoples. But so many different languages have developed that language has often been a barrier rather than an aid to understanding among peoples. For many years, people have dreamed of setting up an international universal language which all people could speak and understand. The arguments in favor of a universal language are simple and obvious. If all peoples spoke the same tongue, cultural and economic ties might be much closer, and good will might increase between countries (Kispert).

Paraphrase
Humans communicate through language. Because there are so many different languages, however, people around the world have a difficult time understanding one another. Some people have wished for a universal international language that speakers all over the world could understand. Their reasons are straightforward and clear. A universal language would build cultural and economic bonds. It would also create better feelings among countries (Kispert).

Source: Kispert, Robert J. “Universal language.” World Book Online Reference Center. 2004. World Book, Inc. 13 Nov. 2004. 原教材来源标注。

Language is the main means of communication between peoples. But so many different languages have developed that language has often been a barrier rather than an aid to understanding among peoples. For many years, people have dreamed of setting up an international universal language which all people could speak and understand. Humans communicate through language. Because there are so many different languages, however, people around the world have a difficult time understanding one another. People communicate through language; however, having different languages creates communication barriers. A universal language could bring countries together culturally and economically as well as increase good feelings among them (Kispert).

Source: Marc Lacey, “Using a New Language in Africa to Save Dying Ones.” New York Times, November 12, 2004, page A3.

Original Passage
Swahili speakers wishing to use a “compyuta”—as computer is rendered in Swahili—have been out of luck when it comes to communicating in their tongue. Computers, no matter how bulky their hard drives or sophisticated their software packages, have not yet mastered Swahili or hundreds of other indigenous African languages. But that may soon change. Across the continent, linguists are working with experts in information technology to make computers more accessible to Africans who happen not to know English, French, or the other major languages that have been programmed into the world’s desktops. There are economic reasons for the outreach. Microsoft, which is working to incorporate Swahili into Microsoft Windows, Microsoft Office, and other popular programs, sees a market for its software among the roughly 100 million Swahili speakers in East Africa. The same goes for Google, which last month launched www.google.co.ke, offering a Kenyan version in Swahili of the popular search engine. But the campaign to Africanize cyberspace is not all about the bottom line. There are hundreds of languages in Africa—some spoken only by a few dozen elders—and they are dying out at an alarming rate. The continent's linguists see the computers as one important way of saving them. UNESCO estimates that 90 percent of the world's 6,000 languages are not represented on the Internet and that one language disappears somewhere around the world every two weeks.

Summary A
People who speak Swahili who want to communicate using a “compyuta,” which is the Swahili word for computer, are unable to do so in their own language. It makes no difference that computers have huge hard drives and sophisticated software. They cannot operate in Swahili or other African languages, of which there are hundreds. Soon, however, they may be able to. Linguists in Africa are working with information technology specialists to make computers operable to Africans who do not know any of the languages currently used on the Internet. Economics is bringing about this change. Microsoft sees a market for its software among Swahili speakers in East Africa. Google now has a search engine for speakers of Swahili in Kenya. Other software companies will probably soon develop products for African consumers. In addition to economics, there is another reason for making the computer accessible to Africans. Hundreds of African languages are dying out, and linguists view the computer as a way to save them. According to UNESCO estimates, 90 percent of the world's 6,000 languages are not on the Internet, and one language becomes extinct every day somewhere in the world. The hope is that computers can help save them (Lacey).

Summary B
Many Africans who do not speak any of the major languages on the Internet have been unable to use computers in their native languages. Computers cannot yet accommodate languages such as Swahili. However, that situation may soon change. Linguists and computer experts are working to develop computers that work in Swahili and other African languages. Economics is one reason for doing so. Computer companies such as Microsoft and Google see a potentially huge market for its products in Africa. Another important reason is to save languages that are in danger of becoming extinct (Lacey).
rubric: 选择B。
说明应概括主旨和主要支撑，而不是尽量保留全部细节。

Source: Various paragraphs of a news article written by Randolph E. Schmid. It was published online by the Associated Press on February 26, 2004. The title of the article is “Share of people who are native English speakers declining.” The article is 25 paragraphs long. The Web site address is <http://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/ap/571281251.html?did=571281251&FMT=ABS&FMTS=FT&date=Feb+26%2C+2004&author=RANDOLPH+E.+SCHMID&desc=Share+of+people+who+are+native+English+speakers+declining.

The world faces a future of people speaking more than one language, with English no longer seen as likely to become dominant, a British language expert says in a new analysis. “English is likely to remain one of the world’s most important languages for the foreseeable future, but its future is more problematic—and complex—than most people appreciate,” said language researcher David Graddol (Schmid, pars. 1-2). He sees English as likely to become the “first among equals” rather than having the global field to itself (par. 3). . . . The share of the world’s population that speaks English as a native language is falling, Graddol reports in a paper in Friday’s issue of the journal Science (par. 5). “There is a distinct consciousness in many countries, both developed and developing, about this dominance of English. There is some evidence of resistance to it, a desire to change it” said [Scott] Montgomery [the author of another article published in the same issue of Science]. For example, he said, in the early years of the Internet it was dominated by sites in English, but in recent years there has been a proliferation of non-English sites, especially Spanish, German, French, Japanese, and others (pars. 19-20). Nonetheless, English is strong as a second language, and teaching it has become a growth industry, said Montgomery, a Seattle-based geologist and energy consultant (par. 21). Graddol noted, though, that employers in parts of Asia are already looking beyond English. “In the next decade the new ‘must learn’ language is likely to be Mandarin” (par. 22).

It [English] is everywhere. Some 380 million people speak it as their first language and perhaps two-thirds as many again as their second. French business schools teach in it. It is the medium of expression in cabinet meetings in Bolivia. Truly, the tongue spoken back in the 1300s only by the “low people” of England, as Robert of Gloucester put it at the time, has come a long way. It is now the global language. How come? Not because English is easy. True, genders are simple, since English relies on “it” as the pronoun for all inanimate nouns, reserving masculine for bona fide males and feminine for females (and countries and ships). But the verbs tend to be irregular, the grammar bizarre, and the match between spelling and pronunciation a nightmare. English is now so widely spoken in so many places that umpteen versions have evolved, some so peculiar that even “native” speakers may have trouble understanding each other. John Simmons, a language consultant for Interbrand, likes to cite the word “set,” an apparently simple word that takes on different meanings in a sporting, cooking, social, or mathematical context—and that is before any little words are combined with it. Then, as a verb, it becomes “set aside,” “set up,” “set down,” “set in,” “set on,” “set about,” “set against,” and so on, terms that “leave even native speakers bewildered about [its] core meaning.”

rules.title: Paraphrase与summary
rules.explanation: paraphrase以自己词汇和句式保留原段的主要信息与必要细节，长度通常相近；summary显著缩短，只保留主旨和主要支撑。两者均不能添加个人观点或改变原义。
rules.example: 原创示例：Original: Regular practice can improve recall. Paraphrase: Learners may remember more effectively through consistent practice.
steps: 先读任务动词：paraphrase要换表达并保留几乎全部信息；summarize要先决定哪些细节可以删。
用一句中文说原文在讲什么，再列主要点和限制。Regular practice can improve recall. 的关键是“经常练习”“可能改善回忆”，不是“必定满分”。
改写时换信息起点或结构；摘要时保留共同主旨，把反复举的例子压缩。
核查some/all、can/will、时间、数字、否定和因果；内容变得更短或更漂亮都不能成为改义理由。
实际借用外部资料时保留来源；本规则的例句明确为原创，不冒充教材引用。

breakdown.note: 原句起点：经常练习。
语气为可能带来改善，不是必然记住一切。
改写转为以学习者为主语，并保留may的可能性。
把练习移到方式短语里，仍保留因果含义。

rules.pitfall: 不要把“改写”当成删句任务，也不要把“摘要”写成逐句换词。先确定任务要保留多大范围。

check.prompt: 【原创理解检查】原句：Some students may benefit from group study. 哪句忠实改写？

options.label: All students will improve if they study together.
Studying with others can help some learners.
Group study is always better than studying alone.

check.explanation: B保留some与may/can。A扩大到所有人并变成必然；C新增比较和always。

rules.title: 两类常见问题
rules.explanation: 没有引用思想来源；虽有引用却只换少数词、保留原句结构。考试判断标签包括Too sim.、No cit.、Inc./Inacc.。
rules.example: 原创示例：may不能改成will，some不能改成all。
steps: 先查来源：能否看到作者、页码/段号或可定位的题名？不能只说“网上有人说”。
再查独立表达：按句子比较主语、谓语和排列顺序。只替换main→principal等几个词，不代表已经用自己的结构重写。

rules.title: 五步改写
rules.explanation: 反复读懂→记关键词而非整句→合上原文写→逐项对照范围、因果、否定、数字与语气→加文内引用。术语可保留，不强求每个词都找近义词。
rules.example: 原创示例：理解原因/结果关系后，再用result from代替because结构。
steps: 第1步反复读到能脱稿解释；只查不懂的词，专业词不必硬换。
第2步记关键词和逻辑箭头，不把整句搬进笔记。
第3步关上原文，依笔记写出完整表达；这样更容易摆脱原句顺序。
第4步打开原文逐点核查：主体、范围、时间、数量、因果、语气是否一致。
第5步补文内引用；作者在引导语出现时，括号按课程要求保留页码或段号。

breakdown.note: 先确定谁引起谁，不只是找近义词。
常把原因接在结果陈述后。
主语是结果，from后接原因；不能把因果方向倒过来。

rules.pitfall: 边盯着原文边替换词，很容易保留整句骨架；只读一遍就写又容易漏信息。用“理解—关键词—合上—核对”分开两种风险。

check.explanation: 先独立写降低贴近原句的风险，再对照核查防止失真；数字与限定是否保留由任务和原义决定。
check.wrongExplanation: 先独立写降低贴近原句的风险，再对照核查防止失真；数字与限定是否保留由任务和原义决定。

rules.title: 同义替换加句法重构
rules.explanation: 主动/被动转换；名词化/动词化；拆句/合句；从句与短语转换；改变信息起点。变化服务于准确，不为改写而扭曲重点。
rules.example: 原创示例：The researchers analyzed the data. → The data were analyzed by the researchers.
steps: 先保留“谁做什么、对象是什么”的事实框架。
可主动改被动：The researchers analyzed the data. → The data were analyzed by the researchers. 主体对象没有互换。
可拆分或合并句子，但原有因果、对比或条件仍须显式保留。
可把名词表达转为动词表达，或改变信息起点；每改一处，都重新问读者能否得到相同意思。
单独做一次被动转换并不保证改写充分；整段仍需独立组织，并保留来源。

breakdown.note: 主动句：研究者是施事，数据是被分析对象。
被动句把对象放到主语位置，改变信息起点。
保持过去时，be + 过去分词构成被动。
原来的行动者仍保留，没有改成“数据分析研究者”。

rules.pitfall: 不能为了避免重复把技术概念换成近似但不同的概念。例如“产生更少钙”与“流失钙”不能不加辨别地当成同一句科学解释。

The researchers will test different samples.

rules.title: 摘要取舍
rules.explanation: 保留研究/文章核心问题、主要发现或主张及必要限制；删去例子、重复、次要数字与修辞。依据题干要求决定是否保留作者名、字数与来源。
rules.example: 原创示例：A passage that gives three examples of review benefits can be summarized by the shared benefit.
steps: 先写一条主旨：作者最终想让读者知道什么？
给各句分工：核心主张、主要理由、例子、重复、细节。摘要保留前两类，后几类通常压缩。
不要把原文没有的合理猜测写进去；“其他公司很快跟进”也需要来源明确说过。
保留会改变结论的限制：可能、部分地区、当时预测、时间范围等。
写完比较长度与覆盖范围：明显短于原文，但不是短到漏掉另一半主旨。

breakdown.note: 三种例子可能只是说明同一个好处，不必逐一复述。
先找例子共同支持的中心意思。
摘要用一句概括共同主旨，但不能新增没有证据的好处。

rules.pitfall: 短不等于好。摘要若把“每两周”写成“每天”、把“可能”写成“必然”，即使很简洁也失真。

options.label: The passage discusses two companies’ services.
All other companies will soon follow them.

check.explanation: C新增对所有其他公司的未来预测；原文没有给出这个判断。
check.wrongExplanation: C新增对所有其他公司的未来预测；原文没有给出这个判断。

rules.sourceLabel: 教材第137–140页；分步讲解与检查题为原创辅助。

rules.title: 作为论据使用
rules.explanation: 先写自己的主题句，再用来源的改写/摘要支撑，随后解释联系。不是把别人的摘要拼在一起替代自己的论证。
rules.example: 原创示例：Frequent review deserves a place in study plans. The supplied passage explains how repeated exposure supports recall. This supports short daily sessions.
steps: 先写自己的主题句，明确你想论证什么，而不是先贴一段来源。
挑与这一主张直接相关的改写或摘要，删去不服务于段落重点的材料。
紧接借用内容给文内引用，使读者分得清来源信息和你的推论。
引用后用自己的句子解释“这说明什么、为什么支持我的观点”。
用结句把证据带回主题；如果拿掉引用，仍应看得出你自己的论证骨架。

breakdown.text: Frequent review deserves a place in study plans.
breakdown.note: 自己的主题句：提出安排复习的主张。

breakdown.text: The supplied passage explains how repeated exposure supports recall.
breakdown.note: 来源提供的证据；实际作答应注明所给来源。
